metadata.narrative: Design a cross-platform anti-cheat system for a competitive first-person shooter video game that could potentially handle up to 1 million concurrent users across multiple game sessions. Requirements: It should have a true positive detection rate of over 98% and a very low false negative detection rate of less than 2%. It should also be lightweight and shouldn't add much overhead to each of the game's builds. Provide a high-level architecture diagram, an outline of your plan, detection pipeline description, cost estimates using cloud/infra prices available currently (July 2025), and a reproducible test methodology. Any non-obvious fact should be followed by a proper source, and/or a inline URL.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A complete design for this anti-cheat system needs an architecture description, a detection pipeline, a cost model, and a reproducible test methodology, grounded in how real anti-cheat systems and cloud infrastructure behave.

The architecture should be layered rather than monolithic, splitting work between a minimal client agent, an authoritative game server, a cloud ingestion/analytics tier, and a human-review tier, because client-side scanning is fast but brittle against new cheats while server-side statistical analysis is slower to activate but has a lower long-run false-positive rate.

Layer one is the client: a thin, Ring-3 agent performing file/process integrity checks only, avoiding a Ring-0 kernel driver, because kernel-level drivers become an attack surface exploitable locally or via a compromised vendor update, and legitimate hardware/software has been wrongly blocked by such checks.

Layer two is the authoritative game server, emitting gameplay telemetry (aim vectors, hit registration, movement, input timing) rather than trusting client-reported state, following the standard login/matchmaking-proxy/game-simulation/database backend pattern.

For 1M concurrent users this tier must be sharded per match/session; comparable production backends have shown a single machine handling roughly 200,000 concurrent connections via efficient async I/O (as in The Division and Titanfall 2) and actor-model frameworks such as Orleans for matchmaking state.

Layer three is cloud ingestion: telemetry flows into a managed stream (Kinesis or MSK) rather than a bespoke pipeline, offering durable, replicated, low-latency ingestion with pay-as-you-go pricing suited to bursty match traffic.

Layer four is detection/inference, split into a cheap always-on statistical model and an expensive deep model reserved for flagged sessions, mirroring Valve's approach of running a lightweight always-on system and reserving heavier ML/human review (Overwatch) for suspicious replays rather than scanning all matches with the expensive model.
Layer five is a human/community review queue, again following the Overwatch pattern, catching statistically ambiguous cases ("skilled player" vs "cheater") before a ban is issued.

The detection pipeline has four stages: client integrity/signature checks; server-side behavioral statistics such as aim ratio, effective-aim duration, and scoped-kill ratio; a deep-learning visual/replay classifier structured as backbone-FPN-classifier (as in VADNet), applied only to flagged sessions; and human/community adjudication.

This staged design is necessary because no single automated layer reliably clears both thresholds: a documented hobbyist neural-network aimbot detector reported only about 91% detection accuracy at 700,000 samples, and even Valve's VACNet has drawn skepticism that no detector is fully immune to an evolving cat-and-mouse dynamic with cheat developers.

Reaching the requested >98% true-positive rate and <2% false-negative rate therefore requires ensembling independent signals so a miss in one layer is caught by another, with rates formally measured through a confusion-matrix framework yielding precision, recall/TPR, F1, and ROC-AUC.

Cross-platform behavior needs explicit handling: input precision differs sharply between mouse/keyboard and controller, and Rust currently keeps PC and console populations segregated specifically because cheating/exploitation risk is judged far higher on the open PC platform than on locked-down consoles.

Detection thresholds and feature weights should therefore be calibrated per input device/platform rather than using one global threshold, with cross-play pools gated behind stricter, platform-aware scoring until sufficient labeled cross-platform data exists.

For cost, ingestion is the first line item: Kinesis charges $0.015 per shard-hour (each shard handling ~1,000 events/sec) plus $0.025 per million PUT payload units, so telemetry at 2 events/sec per player across 1M concurrent players (~2M events/sec) implies roughly 2,000 shards, about $30/hour (~$21,600/month) in shard-hours alone.

An alternative is Amazon MSK, priced per broker-hour ($0.046/hour general-purpose up to $0.234/hour memory-optimized) plus data-transfer-out at $0.09/GB after a small free tier, potentially cheaper at sustained high throughput but requiring more operational expertise.

Inference compute is the second major driver: GPU instances suitable for the deep visual classifier run on the order of $40.96/hour for a multi-GPU configuration, so running that model only on the small fraction of sessions flagged by the cheap statistical stage keeps this cost tractable at 1M-CCU scale.

For the always-on statistical/ensemble models, AWS Graviton3-based C7g CPU instances report up to 50% lower ML inference cost versus comparable c6i/c6g/c5 instances while supporting standard frameworks, making them preferable for the high-volume, low-per-event-cost stage-two model.

Overall, a reasonable mid-2025 monthly estimate is tens of thousands of dollars for streaming ingestion, a comparable or larger sum for GPU inference sized to the flagged-session fraction, and a smaller CPU bill for the always-on statistical layer, though no committed source audits a total at exactly this scale, so this remains a planning estimate.

For reproducible testing, detection accuracy should be evaluated with held-out train/validation/test splits of labeled match telemetry and video, reporting precision, recall/TPR, F1, and full confusion-matrix counts rather than a single accuracy figure.

Scalability and overhead should be verified with bot-driven load tests separating "concurrent users" from "total users," ramping bot count up, holding peak load, then ramping down, using linear/natural/aggressive ramp profiles to mirror realistic traffic bursts.

This should be paired with a repeatable in-game benchmark, analogous to the bot-driven custom-game methodology used to performance-test Overwatch, so client-side overhead is measured under a consistent, replayable battle scenario rather than ad hoc play.

Because the client agent is restricted to lightweight integrity checks with heavy analysis offloaded to the cloud tier, the design follows the same low-footprint philosophy used by security-scanning tools that shift expensive detection work off the endpoint, supporting the low-overhead requirement.

The main evidence gap is that no committed source reports an end-to-end, audited anti-cheat deployment simultaneously hitting exactly >98% TPR and <2% FNR at 1M-CCU scale, so those targets are best treated as validated design goals to be confirmed empirically through the confusion-matrix-based methodology above rather than established facts.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

A complete design for this anti-cheat system needs five parts: an architecture description, a phased plan, a detection pipeline, a cost model, and a reproducible test methodology, all grounded in how real anti-cheat systems and cloud infrastructure actually behave.

The overall architecture should be layered rather than monolithic, splitting work between a minimal client agent, an authoritative game server, a cloud ingestion/analytics tier, and a human-review tier, because industry comparisons show client-side scanning is fast but brittle against new cheats while server-side statistical analysis is slower to activate but has a lower long-run false-positive rate. [shard_01738_70007]
Layer one is the client: a thin, Ring-3 agent that performs file/process integrity checks only, avoiding a Ring-0 kernel driver, because kernel-level anti-cheat drivers themselves become an attack surface that can be exploited locally or through a compromised vendor update, and several documented cases show legitimate hardware/software being wrongly blocked by kernel-level checks. [shard_02982_595]
Layer two is the authoritative game server, which emits gameplay telemetry (aim vectors, hit registration, movement, input timing) rather than trusting client-reported state, following the standard MMO/competitive-game backend pattern of login, matchmaking/proxy, authoritative game-simulation, and database tiers. [shard_05636_67858]
For 1M concurrent users this tier must be horizontally sharded per match/session; comparable production FPS/online backends have shown a single machine handling on the order of 200,000 concurrent connections using efficient async I/O (e.g., IOCP-style designs used by titles like The Division and Titanfall 2, and actor-model frameworks such as Orleans for matchmaking state). [shard_00294_63694]
Layer three is cloud ingestion and stream processing: telemetry is pushed into a managed stream (Kinesis or MSK) rather than a bespoke pipeline, because both offer durable, replicated, low-latency ingestion with pay-as-you-go pricing suited to bursty match traffic. [shard_06482_2120] [shard_01503_74657]
Layer four is the detection/inference tier, split into a cheap always-on statistical model and an expensive deep model reserved for flagged sessions, mirroring Valve's production approach of running a lightweight always-on system and reserving heavier machine-learning/human review (Overwatch) for suspicious replays rather than scanning all 1M+ daily matches with the expensive model. [shard_04049_14138]
Layer five is a human/community review and enforcement queue, again following the Overwatch pattern, which exists specifically to catch cases that are statistically ambiguous ("skilled player" vs "cheater") before an account is banned. [shard_04049_14138]
The detection pipeline itself has four stages: (1) lightweight client integrity/signature checks for known cheat binaries and memory tampering; (2) server-side behavioral statistics such as aim ratio, effective-aim duration, and scoped-kill ratio, which prior work shows separate cheaters from legitimate players; (3) a deep-learning visual/replay classifier, structured as a backbone-FPN-classifier network (similar to VADNet), applied only to sessions flagged by stage two; and (4) human/community adjudication before permanent action. [shard_02021_23222] [shard_04049_14138]
This staged design is necessary because no single automated layer reliably clears both target thresholds: a documented hobbyist neural-network aimbot detector reported only about 91% detection accuracy at 700,000 samples, and even Valve's own machine-learning system (VACNet) has drawn skepticism that no detector is fully immune to an evolving cat-and-mouse dynamic with cheat developers. [shard_03958_37963] [shard_02305_83266]
Reaching the requested >98% true-positive rate and <2% false-negative rate therefore requires ensembling independent signals (client integrity, server statistics, visual replay model, human review) so that a miss in one layer is caught by another, with the target rates formally defined and measured through a confusion-matrix framework (true/false positive and negative counts feeding precision, recall/TPR, F1, and ROC-AUC). [shard_02746_16191]
Cross-platform behavior also needs explicit handling: input precision differs sharply between mouse/keyboard and controller, and other games in this genre (e.g., Rust) currently keep PC and console populations segregated specifically because cheating/exploitation risk is judged far higher on the open PC platform than on locked-down consoles. [shard_04725_75140]
Consequently the detection thresholds and feature weights should be calibrated per input device/platform rather than using one global threshold, with cross-play pools optionally gated behind stricter, platform-aware scoring until sufficient labeled cross-platform data exists.
For cost, ingestion is the first line item: Amazon Kinesis charges $0.015 per shard-hour (each shard handling roughly 1,000 events/sec or 1MB/sec) plus $0.025 per million PUT payload units, so telemetry at even a modest 2 events/sec per player across 1M concurrent players (~2M events/sec) implies roughly 2,000 shards, or about $30/hour (~$21,600/month) in shard-hours alone before payload-unit charges. [shard_06482_2120]
An alternative is Amazon MSK (managed Kafka), priced per broker-hour ($0.046/hour general-purpose up to $0.234/hour memory-optimized) plus data-transfer-out charges of $0.09/GB after a small free tier, which can be cheaper than Kinesis at sustained high throughput but requires more operational expertise. [shard_01503_74657]
Inference compute is the second major cost driver: GPU instances suitable for the deep visual classifier run on the order of $40.96/hour for a multi-GPU configuration, so running the expensive model on only the small fraction of sessions flagged by the cheap statistical stage (rather than all matches) is what keeps this line item tractable at 1M CCU scale. [shard_01190_24840]
For the always-on statistical/ensemble models, AWS Graviton3-based C7g CPU instances report up to 50% lower ML inference cost versus comparable c6i/c6g/c5 instances while supporting standard frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, XGBoost), making them the preferred choice for the high-volume, low-per-event-cost stage-two model. [shard_05768_25267]
Overall, a reasonable current (mid-2025) monthly order-of-magnitude estimate is tens of thousands of dollars for streaming ingestion, a comparable or larger sum for GPU inference sized to the flagged-session fraction, and a smaller CPU-instance bill for the always-on statistical layer, though no committed source gives an audited total for a system precisely at this 1M-CCU scale, so this should be treated as a planning estimate rather than a guaranteed figure. [shard_06482_2120] [shard_01503_74657] [shard_01190_24840]
For reproducible testing, detection accuracy should be evaluated with held-out train/validation/test splits of labeled match telemetry and video, following the same methodology used to validate visual anti-cheat classifiers, reporting precision, recall (TPR), F1, and full confusion-matrix counts rather than a single headline accuracy number. [shard_02021_23222] [shard_02746_16191]
Scalability and overhead should be verified with bot-driven load tests that explicitly separate "concurrent users" from "total users," ramping bot count up, holding peak load, then ramping down, using linear/natural/aggressive ramp profiles to mirror realistic traffic bursts around game launches or tournament peaks. [shard_04910_74474]
This load-testing approach should be paired with a genre-appropriate repeatable in-game benchmark, analogous to the bot-driven custom-game methodology used to performance-test Overwatch, so that client-side CPU/GPU overhead from the anti-cheat agent is measured under a consistent, replayable multiplayer battle scenario rather than ad hoc play sessions. [shard_01358_22940]
Because the client agent is restricted to lightweight signature/integrity checks with heavy analysis offloaded to the cloud tier, the design follows the same low-footprint philosophy used by security-scanning tools that shift expensive detection work off the endpoint, which directly supports the "shouldn't add much overhead to each build" requirement. [shard_05418_25081]
The main evidence gap is that no committed source reports an end-to-end, audited anti-cheat deployment simultaneously hitting exactly >98% TPR and <2% FNR at 1M-CCU scale, so those two targets are best treated as validated design goals to be confirmed empirically through the confusion-matrix-based test methodology described above rather than facts already established in the literature. [shard_02746_16191] [shard_03958_37963]

Layer one is the client: a thin, Ring-3 agent performing file/process integrity checks only, avoiding a Ring-0 kernel driver, because kernel-level drivers become an attack surface exploitable locally or via a compromised vendor update, and legitimate hardware/software has been wrongly blocked by such checks.

Layer two is the authoritative game server, emitting gameplay telemetry (aim vectors, hit registration, movement, input timing) rather than trusting client-reported state, following the standard login/matchmaking-proxy/game-simulation/database backend pattern.

For 1M concurrent users this tier must be sharded per match/session; comparable production backends have shown a single machine handling roughly 200,000 concurrent connections via efficient async I/O (as in The Division and Titanfall 2) and actor-model frameworks such as Orleans for matchmaking state.

Layer three is cloud ingestion: telemetry flows into a managed stream (Kinesis or MSK) rather than a bespoke pipeline, offering durable, replicated, low-latency ingestion with pay-as-you-go pricing suited to bursty match traffic.

Layer four is detection/inference, split into a cheap always-on statistical model and an expensive deep model reserved for flagged sessions, mirroring Valve's approach of running a lightweight always-on system and reserving heavier ML/human review (Overwatch) for suspicious replays rather than scanning all matches with the expensive model.
Layer five is a human/community review queue, again following the Overwatch pattern, catching statistically ambiguous cases ("skilled player" vs "cheater") before a ban is issued.

The detection pipeline has four stages: client integrity/signature checks; server-side behavioral statistics such as aim ratio, effective-aim duration, and scoped-kill ratio; a deep-learning visual/replay classifier structured as backbone-FPN-classifier (as in VADNet), applied only to flagged sessions; and human/community adjudication.

This staged design is necessary because no single automated layer reliably clears both thresholds: a documented hobbyist neural-network aimbot detector reported only about 91% detection accuracy at 700,000 samples, and even Valve's VACNet has drawn skepticism that no detector is fully immune to an evolving cat-and-mouse dynamic with cheat developers.

Reaching the requested >98% true-positive rate and <2% false-negative rate therefore requires ensembling independent signals so a miss in one layer is caught by another, with rates formally measured through a confusion-matrix framework yielding precision, recall/TPR, F1, and ROC-AUC.

Cross-platform behavior needs explicit handling: input precision differs sharply between mouse/keyboard and controller, and Rust currently keeps PC and console populations segregated specifically because cheating/exploitation risk is judged far higher on the open PC platform than on locked-down consoles.

Detection thresholds and feature weights should therefore be calibrated per input device/platform rather than using one global threshold, with cross-play pools gated behind stricter, platform-aware scoring until sufficient labeled cross-platform data exists.

For cost, ingestion is the first line item: Kinesis charges $0.015 per shard-hour (each shard handling ~1,000 events/sec) plus $0.025 per million PUT payload units, so telemetry at 2 events/sec per player across 1M concurrent players (~2M events/sec) implies roughly 2,000 shards, about $30/hour (~$21,600/month) in shard-hours alone.

An alternative is Amazon MSK, priced per broker-hour ($0.046/hour general-purpose up to $0.234/hour memory-optimized) plus data-transfer-out at $0.09/GB after a small free tier, potentially cheaper at sustained high throughput but requiring more operational expertise.

Inference compute is the second major driver: GPU instances suitable for the deep visual classifier run on the order of $40.96/hour for a multi-GPU configuration, so running that model only on the small fraction of sessions flagged by the cheap statistical stage keeps this cost tractable at 1M-CCU scale.

For the always-on statistical/ensemble models, AWS Graviton3-based C7g CPU instances report up to 50% lower ML inference cost versus comparable c6i/c6g/c5 instances while supporting standard frameworks, making them preferable for the high-volume, low-per-event-cost stage-two model.

Overall, a reasonable mid-2025 monthly estimate is tens of thousands of dollars for streaming ingestion, a comparable or larger sum for GPU inference sized to the flagged-session fraction, and a smaller CPU bill for the always-on statistical layer, though no committed source audits a total at exactly this scale, so this remains a planning estimate.

For reproducible testing, detection accuracy should be evaluated with held-out train/validation/test splits of labeled match telemetry and video, reporting precision, recall/TPR, F1, and full confusion-matrix counts rather than a single accuracy figure.

Scalability and overhead should be verified with bot-driven load tests separating "concurrent users" from "total users," ramping bot count up, holding peak load, then ramping down, using linear/natural/aggressive ramp profiles to mirror realistic traffic bursts.

This should be paired with a repeatable in-game benchmark, analogous to the bot-driven custom-game methodology used to performance-test Overwatch, so client-side overhead is measured under a consistent, replayable battle scenario rather than ad hoc play.

Because the client agent is restricted to lightweight integrity checks with heavy analysis offloaded to the cloud tier, the design follows the same low-footprint philosophy used by security-scanning tools that shift expensive detection work off the endpoint, supporting the low-overhead requirement.

The main evidence gap is that no committed source reports an end-to-end, audited anti-cheat deployment simultaneously hitting exactly >98% TPR and <2% FNR at 1M-CCU scale, so those targets are best treated as validated design goals to be confirmed empirically through the confusion-matrix-based methodology above rather than established facts.
